title: Cookies, CSRF & Clickjacking
objectives: Use cookie attributes (Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite, Domain) as defenses
Explain the CSRF token flow and why SameSite is the first line
Protect pages from framing with frame-ancestors and X-Frame-Options
Design state-changing endpoints that cannot be triggered cross-site
body:
Cookies are how the web remembers who you are, and three features make them both convenient and dangerous: the browser attaches them automatically, to every request, including requests some other website triggered. CSRF attacks abuse that automatic attachment; clickjacking abuses what the user sees on top of it. Both have cheap, structural defenses.

## The problem
Your banking-style app uses a session cookie with no attributes set, and a state-changing `POST /transfer` that accepts form bodies. A malicious site can post that form while the user is logged in — the cookie rides along and the server cannot tell the request apart from a legitimate one.

## Constraints
- `HttpOnly` hides the cookie from JavaScript (blunts XSS exfiltration); `Secure` restricts it to HTTPS; `SameSite` governs cross-site sending.
- `SameSite=Lax` sends the cookie on top-level navigations but not on cross-site form posts or fetches; `Strict` blocks even navigations.
- `Domain=example.com` makes a cookie visible to every subdomain — broader scope is broader blast radius.
- CSRF tokens work because the attacker's site cannot read your pages or tokens (SOP); they can only cause requests, not observe them.
- Framing defenses: CSP `frame-ancestors` controls who may embed the page; `X-Frame-Options` is the legacy fallback.

## Options
```txt
# Defense 1: hardened session cookie (first line)
Set-Cookie: sid=8f3k...; Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax; Path=/; Max-Age=3600

# Defense 2: synchronizer token on state-changing requests (second line)
GET  /transfer-form  ->  <input type=hidden name=csrf value=r4nd0m-per-session>
POST /transfer       ->  server compares form csrf to session csrf; mismatch = reject

# Defense 3: framing protection (clickjacking)
Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'
X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN
```
SameSite stops most cross-site posts from carrying the cookie at all; the token catches what SameSite does not (older browsers, Lax-allowed navigations); framing protection stops invisible-overlay attacks on the pages that do load.

## Tradeoffs
`SameSite=Strict` breaks legitimate cross-site entry links (email links lose the session) — `Lax` is the pragmatic default. Synchronizer tokens add server state or double-submit machinery per form. `frame-ancestors` needs CSP support; old browsers still rely on `X-Frame-Options`, so production sets both.

## Decision
Set `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax` on every session cookie, keep `Domain` unset unless subdomain sharing is required. Require a CSRF token for every state-changing request that can be triggered by form or fetch, and reject requests whose Origin/Referer is cross-site. Serve `frame-ancestors 'self'` (plus XFO) on all authenticated pages.

## Measure it
Test like an attacker, defensively: from a page on another origin, attempt a form post and a fetch to each state-changing endpoint and assert rejection (403/token mismatch) — with and without a stolen valid cookie. Assert cookie headers in integration tests: attributes present exactly as specified. Load each authenticated page in an iframe from a foreign origin and assert the browser refuses to render it.

## Best practices
- Ship session cookies as `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Lax` at minimum.
- Require CSRF tokens on all state-changing routes; prefer synchronizer or double-submit patterns.
- Validate Origin/Referer on state-changing requests as a second signal.
- Set `Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors 'self'` on authenticated pages.
- Keep cookie scope narrow: no blanket `Domain` attribute unless you need it.

## Common mistakes
- Relying on the token but shipping the cookie without SameSite, so any subdomain XSS or old browser reopens the hole.
- Putting CSRF tokens on GET links, which leak them via Referer headers and browser history.
- Setting `Domain=.example.com` for convenience and exposing the session to every subdomain, including a compromised one.
- Forgetting X-Frame-Options/frame-ancestors on pages whose buttons matter, allowing clickjacking overlays.
- Treating CORS headers as CSRF protection — CORS cannot stop the request from being *sent*.

## Production considerations
- Rotate CSRF tokens per session (and per form for high-value actions like password change or transfer).
- Monitor 403 token-mismatch spikes: they are either a broken deploy or an active CSRF/crawler wave — both worth knowing.
- Legacy-browser requirements may force checking tokens server-side even when SameSite would nominally cover you; keep the token layer regardless.
- Audit cookie inventory (name, attributes, scope) on a schedule; stray tracking or debug cookies are the usual drift.

examples.name: csrf-flow.txt
examples.code:
CSRF defense flow (synchronizer pattern), step by step

1. GET /transfer-form
   server: session found, generates token t=7c1f..., stores in session,
           embeds in form:
           <form method=POST action=/transfer>
             <input type=hidden name=csrf value=7c1f...>
           </form>

2. Attacker site hosts: <form action=https://bank.example/transfer method=POST>
   ... and submits it while the victim is logged in.
   Browser attaches the session cookie (SameSite=Lax does NOT attach it for
   cross-site POSTs; this is the first line failing open on old browsers).

3. POST /transfer arrives with cookie but WITHOUT the valid csrf field
   (the attacker cannot read the token: Same-Origin Policy blocks it).
   server: session.csrf (7c1f...) !== form.csrf (absent) -> 403 reject.

Layered outcome:
  SameSite=Lax   -> request never carries the cookie (modern browsers)
  CSRF token     -> server rejects what SameSite misses
  frame-ancestors-> attacker cannot overlay the real page to fake clicks

exercise.prompt: Audit cookies and endpoints. For each cookie, render a verdict listing missing defenses: session cookie needs Secure, HttpOnly and SameSite; a tracking cookie without HttpOnly is fine, but one with Domain=.example.com is over-scoped. For the endpoints, POST /transfer without CSRF protection must be flagged. Implement the auditor.
hints: Collect the missing attributes into one string per cookie: Secure, HttpOnly, SameSite.
A Domain=.example.com cookie is over-scoped regardless of other attributes.
Only state-changing methods (POST/PUT/DELETE) need CSRF checks.

questions.prompt: Why does SameSite=Lax prevent most CSRF attacks?
options: It stops the cookie from being attached to cross-site POST requests
It blocks all cross-site requests in the browser
It makes the cookie visible only to JavaScript on the same origin
questions.explanation: CSRF needs the session cookie to ride along on the forged request; Lax cookies are withheld from cross-site form posts and fetches, breaking most attacks at the source.

questions.prompt: Which header pair defends a page against clickjacking?
questions.explanation: Clickjacking embeds your page in an attacker-controlled iframe; frame-ancestors and X-Frame-Options tell the browser to refuse that framing.
